segments.title: PKM Deep Dive
segments.content:
Mastering Personal Knowledge Management

Your Avatar's intelligence is only as good as the knowledge you feed it. This segment explores advanced PKM strategies.

The PKM Pyramid

  1. Capture Layer: Raw inputs—meeting notes, web clippings, voice memos, and screenshots. Quantity matters here.
  2. Process Layer: Distilled notes, summaries, and tagged highlights. This is where you add your own insights.
  3. Retrieve Layer: Structured folders, linked documents, and indexed metadata. The Avatar searches here.
  4. Create Layer: Outputs generated from retrieved knowledge—reports, emails, and presentations.

Case Study: The Researcher Who Never Forgot

Dr. Elena Voss, a pharmaceutical researcher, reads 40+ papers monthly. Before Zetrix, she relied on scattered PDFs and handwritten notes. After building her PKM Pyramid:

  • Capture: She clips every paper summary using the Zetrix browser extension.
  • Process: Each Sunday, she spends 30 minutes writing 3-bullet takeaways for each clip.
  • Retrieve: Her Avatar answers complex queries like "What papers mention kinase inhibitors and liver toxicity?" in seconds.
  • Create: Grant proposals now draft themselves from her curated knowledge base.

Result: Proposal writing time cut from 2 weeks to 3 days. She won 3 new grants in 12 months.

Framework: The 10-Minute Capture Ritual

Build this into your daily routine. Set a timer:

  • Minutes 0–2: Open your "00 – Inbox" folder. Review what you captured today.
  • Minutes 2–6: For each item, decide: Process now, Archive, or Delete.
  • Minutes 6–9: Write 1–2 sentences summarising the key insight. Tag with relevant keywords.
  • Minutes 9–10: Move processed items to their permanent folder. Inbox = empty.

Golden Rule: Capture without judgment, process with intention, retrieve with precision.

segments.title: Document Upload Workflows
segments.content:
Efficient Document Ingestion

Uploading documents is easy. Uploading them so the Avatar understands them is an art. Here is the workflow.

Step-by-Step: Preparing Documents for Upload

  1. Clean the source: Remove headers, footers, and page numbers from PDFs. They confuse retrieval.
  2. Use descriptive filenames: "2026-Q3-Sales-Report-v2.pdf" beats "report-final-FINAL.pdf."
  3. Add a cover page summary: For long documents, include a 1-paragraph summary at the top. The Avatar weights top content heavily.
  4. Convert images to text: If a document contains charts with key data, add a text appendix explaining the numbers.
  5. Batch upload by topic: Upload all marketing documents in one session. The Avatar builds a richer context cluster.
  6. Verify extraction: After upload, click "Preview Text." If tables are garbled, re-export as a cleaner PDF.
  7. Set metadata: Add author, date, and topic tags in the PKM Manager sidebar.

Supported Formats and Tips

  • PDF: Best for static documents. Ensure text is selectable, not scanned images.
  • DOCX: Ideal for editable content. The Avatar preserves heading structure for better navigation.
  • Markdown (MD): Perfect for structured notes. Supports links, code blocks, and tables natively.
  • CSV/XLSX: Use for data-heavy content. The Avatar can query specific rows during retrieval.

Case Study: The Lawyer’s Document Pipeline

James, a corporate lawyer, uploads 20–30 contracts weekly. His old system: dump everything in one folder. Retrieval was a nightmare. His new workflow:

  1. Renames every file: "Client-ContractType-Date-vX."
  2. Adds a 3-sentence summary at the top of each document.
  3. Tags with: client name, contract type, value tier, and risk level.
  4. Uploads in batches by client to build context clusters.

Now his Avatar retrieves relevant clauses in 3 seconds. Contract review time: down 60%.

Framework: The PREP Checklist

Before uploading any document, run PREP:

  • P – Purge: Remove irrelevant pages, headers, and footers.
  • R – Rename: Use descriptive, dated filenames.
  • E – Explain: Add a summary at the top.
  • P – Preview: Check extracted text for errors.

segments.title: Advanced Folder Organisation
segments.content:
Scaling Your PKM Beyond 100 Documents

As your knowledge base grows, flat folders collapse. Here is how to organise at scale.

The PARA Method (Adapted for AI)

  1. Projects: Folders with a deadline and outcome. Example: "Launch New Website – Aug 2026." Close them when done.
  2. Areas: Ongoing responsibilities without a deadline. Example: "Health," "Finance," "Team Management."
  3. Resources: Reference material you might need someday. Example: "UX Design Patterns," "Tax Law 2026."
  4. Archive: Completed projects and outdated resources. Keeps active folders lean.

Step-by-Step: Reorganising an Existing PKM

  1. Export a list of all documents from the PKM Manager.
  2. Create four new top-level folders: 01-Projects, 02-Areas, 03-Resources, 04-Archive.
  3. Sort each existing document into one of the four categories. Be ruthless—if in doubt, choose Archive.
  4. Inside Projects, create subfolders named with a deadline prefix: "2026-08 – Website Launch."
  5. Inside Areas, create subfolders for each responsibility. Add a recurring review note.
  6. Tag every document with a primary and secondary keyword.
  7. Test retrieval: Ask the Avatar a question that spans multiple folders and verify it synthesises correctly.

Case Study: From 400 Files to Organised Bliss

Maria, a freelance designer, had 400 files in one "Work" folder. Finding anything took 5+ minutes. After applying PARA:

  • Projects: 12 active client folders with clear deadlines.
  • Areas: "Invoicing," "Marketing," "Skill Development."
  • Resources: "Typography Guides," "Colour Theory," "Contract Templates."
  • Archive: 200+ completed projects moved out of the way.

Retrieval time: under 10 seconds. Stress level: significantly lower.

Deep Dive: The Archive Rule

Archive is not a trash can. It is a reference library. The key difference: Archived documents are excluded from active retrieval but remain searchable when explicitly requested. This keeps your Avatar's "working memory" lean and fast.

Pro Tip: Review your folder structure every 90 days. What made sense in January may be obsolete by April.

segments.title: Daily Updates & Memory Refresh
segments.content:
Turning Information into Memory

Daily Updates are not just news feeds—they are memory reinforcement loops. This segment shows you how to optimise them.

How Memory Works in Your Avatar

  1. Encoding: New information enters via uploads, Daily Updates, or conversation.
  2. Consolidation: The Avatar links new data to existing knowledge during idle periods (usually overnight).
  3. Retrieval: When you ask a question, the Avatar searches indexed memory and ranks relevance.
  4. Reinforcement: Frequently accessed memories are prioritised. Rarely used data fades but is not deleted.

Step-by-Step: Optimising Daily Updates

  1. Open Daily Updates > Sources and review current feeds. Remove any source that has not provided value in 2 weeks.
  2. Add a manual reflection source. Each evening, type or dictate 3 bullets: what you learned, what you decided, and what you need tomorrow.
  3. Enable cross-linking in settings. This tells the Avatar to connect new updates to existing documents automatically.
  4. Set a weekly memory review. Every Sunday, ask: "What did I learn this week?" The Avatar synthesises highlights.
  5. Use memory pinning for critical facts. Click the pin icon next to any retrieved result to keep it permanently accessible.

Case Study: The Executive Who Never Missed a Beat

Thomas, a CTO at a fintech startup, receives 200+ Slack messages and 50+ emails daily. Before Daily Updates, he missed context constantly. His setup now:

  • Morning briefing (08:00): Summary of overnight commits, Jira ticket changes, and key Slack threads.
  • Midday pulse (12:30): Calendar preview for afternoon meetings, with relevant PKM documents attached.
  • Evening reflection (18:00): He dictates 3 bullets. The Avatar links them to relevant projects and surfaces them in tomorrow's briefing.

"I used to spend 90 minutes catching up every morning. Now I'm informed in 90 seconds," Thomas reports.

Example Reflection: "Learned: AI agents need clear boundaries. Decided: Limit my sales agent to 3 email templates. Need tomorrow: Q3 budget spreadsheet."

Framework: The Spaced Repetition Loop

Your Avatar can reinforce your own memory, not just its own. Ask it to:

  • Quiz you on yesterday's reflections.
  • Surface last week's decisions before this week's planning.
  • Connect today's news to last month's learnings.

segments.title: Identity Model Mastery
segments.content:
Refining Your Avatar's Core Self

An Identity Model is never finished. It evolves as you evolve. Here is how to refine it based on real interactions.

Step-by-Step: Identity Audit

  1. Navigate to Avatar Profile > Identity Model > Audit.
  2. Review the last 50 interactions. The system flags responses where the Avatar seemed off-tone or off-topic.
  3. For each flagged interaction, ask: Did this match my values? Was the tone right? Was it too verbose?
  4. Edit the Core Values section. Add clarifying sentences. Example: "When giving feedback, start with a specific strength, then one improvement."
  5. Update your bio with recent milestones. If you changed jobs or goals, the Avatar needs to know.
  6. Adjust communication preferences. If you find yourself asking for shorter answers, lower the default response length.
  7. Save and test. Ask a sample question and compare the new response to an old one.

Case Study: The Evolving Entrepreneur

Alex started Zetrix as a solo founder. His Identity Model bio said: "Building a SaaS MVP, seeking product-market fit." Six months later, he had 50 customers and 2 employees. But his Avatar was still giving "MVP advice"—build fast, ship broken, iterate daily. This clashed with his new reality: he needed stability, customer support, and team coordination.

After updating his bio to "Scaling a SaaS from 50 to 500 customers. Focus: retention, team processes, and predictable releases," his Avatar's advice transformed. It now suggested onboarding sequences, hiring playbooks, and release management.

Lesson: Your Identity Model is a living document. Review it monthly, or it will give you advice from your past.

Advanced: Adding Role-Specific Identities

You can create multiple identity profiles within one Avatar:

  • Work Mode: Direct, data-driven, concise.
  • Creative Mode: Exploratory, metaphorical, long-form.
  • Coach Mode: Supportive, question-based, patient.

Switch modes by saying: "Switch to Coach Mode." The Avatar loads the relevant identity subset instantly.

Framework: The Identity Delta

Track the gap between your ideal self and your Avatar's current behaviour:

  1. Write down 3 traits your ideal assistant would have. (e.g., "Proactive," "Concise," "Encouraging")
  2. Score your Avatar 1–10 on each trait.
  3. For any score below 7, edit the Identity Model to close the gap.
  4. Re-score in 2 weeks. Repeat.

segments.title: Voice Training & Speech Patterns
segments.content:
Making Your Avatar Sound Like You

Voice cloning is the start. Speech pattern training makes the Avatar truly indistinguishable.

Step-by-Step: Advanced Voice Training

  1. Record a variety of samples:
    • A professional introduction (30 sec)
    • A casual story about your weekend (60 sec)
    • A technical explanation of your work (45 sec)
    • An emotional message—excited or concerned (30 sec)
  2. Upload all samples in the Voice > Advanced Training section.
  3. Label each sample with its context tag: professional, casual, technical, emotional.
  4. Enable context-aware voice selection. The Avatar now picks the right tone for the right situation.
  5. Test with prompts:
    • "Explain quantum computing" → should use technical tone
    • "Tell me a joke" → should use casual tone
    • "I just got promoted!" → should use emotional/excited tone
  6. Fine-tune pacing. In Voice Settings, adjust words-per-minute for each context. Match your natural speed.

Case Study: The Voice Actor's Surprise

Lisa, a professional voice actor, was sceptical about AI voice cloning. She uploaded 4 samples: commercial, audiobook, character voice, and conversational. After training:

  • Her Avatar could read scripts in her "commercial" voice for ad clients.
  • It could narrate long articles in her "audiobook" voice.
  • It could answer casual questions in her natural conversational tone.

She now uses it for first-pass auditions, saving 10+ hours weekly. Clients cannot tell the difference between AI-generated samples and her live recordings.

Speech Pattern Customisation

  • Filler words: Add or remove "um," "you know," and "actually" to match your style.
  • Pauses: Set pause length after sentences and paragraphs. Longer pauses feel more thoughtful.
  • Emphasis: Teach the Avatar which words you naturally stress. Use bold markers in training transcripts.

Framework: The Voice Consistency Score

Rate your Avatar's voice on these 5 dimensions (1–10):

  1. Clarity – Can you understand every word?
  2. Likeness – Does it sound like YOU?
  3. Appropriateness – Is the tone right for the context?
  4. Emotion – Does it convey the right feeling?
  5. Pacing – Is the speed natural?

Any score below 7 = retrain that dimension.

segments.title: Memory Architecture
segments.content:
How Your Avatar Remembers

Memory is not a black box. Understanding the architecture lets you optimise what sticks and what fades.

Three Memory Tiers

  1. Working Memory (Session): Lasts for the current conversation. Holds 8–12 recent turns. Used for immediate context.
  2. Episodic Memory (Daily Updates): Stores events, decisions, and reflections from the past 90 days. Used for "what did I do last week?" questions.
  3. Semantic Memory (PKM): Long-term knowledge from documents and structured data. Used for expertise and facts.

Step-by-Step: Memory Optimisation

  1. Check Memory Stats in the Avatar Profile. Review memory distribution across tiers.
  2. If Working Memory is overloaded (long conversations), break chats into topics. Start a new thread for each subject.
  3. If Episodic Memory is thin, increase Daily Update frequency. Add manual reflections every evening.
  4. If Semantic Memory is bloated, archive documents older than 12 months. The Avatar retrieves faster with a leaner index.
  5. Use memory tags to link related items. Tag a project document and a meeting note with the same keyword to create a cluster.
  6. Run a memory defrag monthly. This reorganises the index and removes orphaned references.

Case Study: The Memory Doctor

Dr. Patel, a general practitioner, uploaded 500+ medical guidelines to his Avatar. Retrieval slowed to 8 seconds. After optimisation:

  • Archived guidelines older than 2 years.
  • Added tags for body system, condition severity, and patient age group.
  • Started new chat threads per patient case.

Retrieval time: under 2 seconds. Patient consultation efficiency: up 25%.

Deep Dive: Memory Decay Curves

Not all memories are equal. Zetrix uses a decay algorithm:

  • High-access memories (retrieved daily) stay in fast cache.
  • Medium-access memories (retrieved weekly) move to standard index.
  • Low-access memories (retrieved monthly) are archived but still searchable.
  • Pinned memories bypass decay entirely. Use sparingly for critical facts.

Example Question per Tier:

  • Working: "What did I just ask?"
  • Episodic: "What did we decide about the budget in last Tuesday's meeting?"
  • Semantic: "What are the three pillars of our marketing strategy?"

segments.title: Retrieval & Search Techniques
segments.content:
Finding Exactly What You Need

Even the best-organised PKM is useless if you cannot find things. Master these retrieval techniques.

Basic Retrieval Commands

  1. Keyword search: "Find documents about Q3 budget."
  2. Date filter: "Show me meeting notes from July 2026."
  3. Author filter: "What did Sarah write about onboarding?"
  4. Type filter: "List all spreadsheets in the Finance folder."

Advanced Retrieval Techniques

  1. Cross-document synthesis: "Compare the Q2 and Q3 sales reports. What changed?" The Avatar reads both and produces a diff.
  2. Question-driven retrieval: "Why did we choose React over Vue?" The Avatar searches decision logs and meeting notes.
  3. Hypothetical retrieval: "If we had doubled the marketing budget, what would the plan say?" The Avatar finds the budget sensitivity analysis.
  4. Temporal retrieval: "What was my opinion on remote work a year ago?" The Avatar searches old reflections and notes.

Step-by-Step: Testing Retrieval Accuracy

  1. Pick a document you know exists. Ask a question that requires it.
  2. Review the Avatar's answer. Did it cite the right source?
  3. If not, check the document's tags and folder. Move or retag for better discoverability.
  4. Add a retrieval hint in the document's first paragraph. Example: "This document covers the 2026 marketing budget and ROI projections."
  5. Re-test after 5 minutes. The index updates quickly.

Case Study: The Lawyer Who Won with Retrieval

Sophie, a litigation lawyer, had 2,000+ case documents. Before mastering retrieval, she manually searched folders for hours. Her breakthrough techniques:

  • Cross-document synthesis: "Compare the witness statements from Case A and Case B. Flag contradictions."
  • Temporal retrieval: "Show me all motions filed in the 30 days before the trial date."
  • Retrieval hints: She added a 1-sentence summary at the top of every document.

Case preparation time: reduced by 45%. She won a major case partly because her Avatar surfaced a precedent she had forgotten.

Framework: The Retrieval Funnel

Structure your searches from broad to narrow:

  1. Broad: "What do I know about marketing?"
  2. Filtered: "Show me marketing documents from Q3 2026."
  3. Specific: "What did the Q3 marketing budget say about paid social?"
  4. Synthetic: "Compare Q3 paid social results to Q2. What changed?"

segments.title: Linking Knowledge & Building Graphs
segments.content:
Connecting Ideas for Deeper Intelligence

Isolated documents are facts. Linked documents are understanding. This segment teaches you to build a knowledge graph.

What Is a Knowledge Graph?

A knowledge graph connects documents, people, projects, and concepts via relationships. Example: "Document A mentions Project B, which is owned by Person C, who reports to Person D."

Step-by-Step: Creating Links

  1. In the PKM Manager, open any document and click Add Link.
  2. Choose the link type: references, contradicts, supports, parent of, or child of.
  3. Select the target document from the search box.
  4. Add a link note explaining the connection. Example: "This budget supports the marketing plan in Document B."
  5. Save the link. It now appears in both documents' link panels.
  6. View the Graph Visualiser from the PKM sidebar. Zoom in to see local clusters; zoom out to see the whole knowledge map.

Automated Linking

  1. Enable Auto-Link in PKM Settings.
  2. The Avatar scans new uploads and suggests links based on shared keywords, authors, and dates.
  3. Review suggestions weekly. Approve good ones, reject irrelevant ones.
  4. Over time, the graph becomes self-organising. The Avatar predicts connections before you make them.

Case Study: The Product Manager's Graph

Hassan, a product manager at a SaaS company, built a knowledge graph connecting:

  • User research documents → linked to feature specs (supports relationship)
  • Feature specs → linked to engineering tickets (parent of relationship)
  • Competitor analysis → linked to strategy docs (references relationship)
  • Post-mortems → linked to project plans (contradicts relationship, showing lessons learned)

When his CEO asked, "Why did we prioritise Feature X over Feature Y?" Hassan traced the graph in 30 seconds: user research → feature spec → strategy doc. The answer was crystal clear.

Framework: The LINK Method

When adding a link, always include:

  • L – Label: What type of link is this? (references, supports, contradicts)
  • I – Insight: Why does this connection matter?
  • N – Note: A 1-sentence explanation.
  • K – Keep current: Review links quarterly. Remove stale ones.

Benefit: When you ask "What do I know about X?" the Avatar traverses the graph and returns connected insights, not just isolated facts.

segments.title: 30-Day Brain Challenge
segments.content:
Building an Unstoppable Knowledge System

This challenge transforms your Avatar from a chatbot into a true second brain. Commit to 30 days.

Week 1: Capture Everything

  1. Day 1: Install the browser extension and clip 5 articles.
  2. Day 2: Upload all documents from your Downloads folder. Sort into PARA folders.
  3. Day 3: Record 3 voice memos and let the Avatar transcribe them.
  4. Day 4: Add one RSS feed and one newsletter source to Daily Updates.
  5. Day 5: Write your first evening reflection. 3 bullets only.
  6. Day 6: Create links between 3 pairs of related documents.
  7. Day 7: Ask the Avatar: "Summarise my week." Review accuracy.

Week 2: Retrieve with Precision

  1. Day 8–10: Ask 5 complex questions daily. Note which ones fail.
  2. Day 11–12: Fix failed retrievals by retagging, moving, or summarising documents.
  3. Day 13–14: Test cross-document synthesis. Ask comparison and trend questions.

Week 3: Automate & Integrate

  1. Day 15–17: Connect Gmail and Slack. Let the Avatar auto-file messages.
  2. Day 18–19: Build a custom agent that answers FAQs using your PKM.
  3. Day 20–21: Enable Auto-Link and review 10 suggested connections.

Week 4: Reflect & Scale

  1. Day 22–24: Review memory stats. Archive old documents.
  2. Day 25–27: Refine Identity Model based on 3 weeks of usage.
  3. Day 28–29: Teach a teammate to use your PKM structure.
  4. Day 30: Export a knowledge report. Celebrate your second brain.

Success Metrics

  • Documents captured: Target 50+ by Day 30.
  • Links created: Target 20+ connections.
  • Retrieval accuracy: 80%+ of complex questions answered correctly.
  • Time saved: Track hours reclaimed from automated filing and synthesis.

Mindset: Your Avatar's brain is a garden. Tend it daily, prune monthly, and harvest insights on demand.
